title: Updated A(H1N1)pdm09 influenza virus ferret infection model permits refined antiviral assessment using aerosol inhalation challenge.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Seasonal influenza viruses continue to pose a significant threat to human health. As influenza viruses exhibit sustained genetic drift, it is imperative that animal studies utilize challenge strains that reflect contemporary, currently circulating viruses when evaluating pathogenicity, viral tropism, transmissibility, and antiviral sensitivity to better inform public health responses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Ferrets are considered the gold-standard small animal model for assessing currently circulating influenza viruses. Utilising representative influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 virus strains from 2009 to 2022, we explored virus replication kinetics and lung pathogenesis in ferrets following intranasal inoculation with these contemporary strains.
analysis.methods: To refine this updated model, we performed side-by-side evaluation of oseltamivir antiviral efficacy following traditional intranasal or aerosol inhalation influenza challenges.
analysis.main_results: Our results revealed strain specific differences, with greater lung viral loads and pathogenesis following inoculation with A/Sydney/5/2021 compared to other strains. Pre-treatment with oseltamivir demonstrated greater reductions in viral shedding from the upper respiratory tract than post-infection treatment of ferrets infected by aerosol inhalation, while the intranasal route showed reduced oseltamivir efficacy independent of the timing of antiviral treatment.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings provide the basis for using an updated A(H1N1)pdm09 challenge virus for ferret studies as an alternative to the commonly used, but now less relevant 2009 early pandemic viruses. It also highlights how different methods of virus inoculation can influence outcomes of ferret antiviral studies, with an aerosol challenge model able to demonstrate differences between therapeutic and prophylactic treatments, which were not apparent with an intranasal challenge model.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Efficient transmissibility of A/Sydney/5/2021 virus to naïve recipients was also observed following both contact and airborne exposure to infected donor ferrets. This study provides a refined model for evaluating antiviral efficacy against contemporary A(H1N1)pdm09 strains, which can inform improved therapeutic strategies and vaccine development.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report limitations of the study design. The evidence strength is high as the study directly compares contemporary A(H1N1)pdm09 strains and evaluates antiviral efficacy using both intranasal and aerosol challenge models.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to refine the ferret infection model for assessing antiviral efficacy against contemporary A(H1N1)pdm09 influenza viruses. The researchers evaluated virus replication kinetics and lung pathogenesis in ferrets using strains from 2009 to 2022, highlighting the importance of using updated challenge strains to reflect current circulating viruses. They performed side-by-side comparisons of oseltamivir efficacy following intranasal and aerosol inhalation challenges, revealing strain-specific differences in viral load and pathogenesis. The results showed that A/Sydney/5/2021 had higher lung viral loads compared to other strains, and pre-treatment with oseltamivir was more effective in reducing upper respiratory viral shedding than post-infection treatment. The aerosol challenge model demonstrated differences between therapeutic and prophylactic treatments, which were not evident with the intranasal model. These findings support the use of updated A(H1N1)pdm09 strains for ferret studies, offering a more accurate representation of current viral behavior and informing improved antiviral strategies. The study's evidence strength is high due to its direct comparison of contemporary strains and evaluation of different challenge methods.

title: Sex and age differences in antibody responses to seasonal influenza vaccination are mediated by estrogenic upregulation of NF-κB and TNF signaling in B cells.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate how age-related changes, including hormonal fluctuations, influence sex differences in antibody responses to seasonal influenza vaccination, particularly in young adults and old adults.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed sex differences in humoral immune responses to the seasonal quadrivalent influenza vaccine (QIV) in young adults (YA; 18-49 years old) and old adults (OA; 75+ years old), focusing on antibody titers and B-cell subsets post-vaccination.
analysis.methods: Machine learning algorithms were used to identify baseline steroids and B-cell markers as predictors of seroconversion at 28 days post-vaccination, while single-cell RNA sequencing examined transcriptional activity and gene expression in CD19+ B cells.
analysis.main_results: In YA females, estradiol treatment increased HA+ IgG+ cells and ERE gene expression along the NF-κB-mediated TNF signaling pathway, an effect inhibited by an estrogen receptor antagonist. These effects were not observed in YA males or OA groups.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that estrogen signaling enhances antibody secretion in YA females through NF-κB and TNF pathways, and that these sex differences diminish with age due to hormonal changes.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide insights into the biological mechanisms underlying sex differences in vaccine responses and highlight the role of the hormonal environment in shaping immune outcomes to seasonal influenza.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on ex vivo experiments and does not account for in vivo complexities, which may limit the generalizability of findings. However, the use of machine learning and single-cell RNA sequencing provides strong mechanistic evidence.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores how sex differences in antibody responses to seasonal influenza vaccination are influenced by estrogenic upregulation of NF-κB and TNF signaling in B cells. It focuses on young adults (YA) and old adults (OA), revealing that YA females exhibit stronger immune responses due to elevated estrogen levels, which enhance B-cell activity and antibody production. These effects are mediated through estrogen receptor engagement and are mitigated in OA, suggesting a hormonal basis for age-related changes in vaccine immunity. The study uses machine learning and single-cell RNA sequencing to identify key predictors and transcriptional changes, offering mechanistic insights into sex differences in influenza vaccine responses. While the findings are based on ex vivo experiments, they provide a strong foundation for understanding how hormonal environments shape immune outcomes. The results have implications for vaccine development and personalized immunization strategies, particularly for reproductive-aged females.

title: A novel ursodeoxycholic acid derivative exhibits broad-spectrum antiviral activity against influenza A virus and coronaviruses by multiphasic disruption of the viral life cycle.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the limitations of current antiviral agents, which are narrow-spectrum and prone to drug resistance, by developing a broad-spectrum antiviral agent effective against influenza A and B viruses and human coronaviruses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study characterized a novel ursodeoxycholic acid derivative (U-BSA) in vitro and in vivo against influenza A viruses (H1N1 and H3N2), human coronaviruses (HCoVs), and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).
analysis.methods: U-BSA was tested for antiviral activity against influenza A viruses, HCoVs, and RSV using in vitro assays and a lethal influenza infection model in vivo. Mechanistic studies were conducted to understand the mode of action.
analysis.main_results: U-BSA exhibited inhibitory activity against H1N1 (EC50 = 4.10 μM, SI > 50), H3N2 (EC50 = 2.41 μM, SI > 40), HCoV-OC43 (EC50 = 9.66 μM, SI > 20), and RSV (EC50 = 6.01 μM, SI > 12). It also provided significant protection in a lethal influenza infection model in vivo.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: U-BSA interferes with multiple viral life cycles, including viral attachment, endosomal acidification, and virion release, and rescues virus-induced membrane lipid disorder, making it a promising candidate for broad-spectrum antivirals.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that U-BSA could be a valuable tool for combating pan-respiratory viruses, enhancing therapeutic efficacy and overcoming drug resistance.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the use of in vitro and in vivo models, which may not fully represent the complexity of human infections. The sample size for in vivo studies was small, and the generalizability of the findings is uncertain.

analysis.summary_en: This study developed a novel ursodeoxycholic acid derivative (U-BSA) that exhibits broad-spectrum antiviral activity against influenza A and B viruses and human coronaviruses. U-BSA interferes with multiple viral life cycles and rescues virus-induced membrane lipid disorder, making it a promising candidate for broad-spectrum antivirals.

title: Antivirals for seasonal influenza in the US: modeling direct and indirect effects with variable uptake

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza antivirals can directly benefit treated individuals by reducing the risk of some influenza-associated complications when initiated soon after symptom onset.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The supplied evidence does not clearly state the study design, setting, or study population.
analysis.methods: Using a compartmental framework, we modeled population-level reductions in influenza-associated hospitalizations given potential direct and indirect effects of influenza antivirals in the United States.
analysis.main_results: From reported patterns of care-seeking, antiviral prescribing, and treatment adherence, we estimated 1.1-9.7% of symptomatic individuals initiate and adhere to prompt antiviral treatment.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: For example, up to 3.8% of hospitalizations were prevented when antivirals reduced hospitalization risk and onward transmission by 20%.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: More substantial impacts (for example, preventing >20% of hospitalizations) were only achieved by increasing initiation and adherence to prompt treatment beyond typically observed levels.

analysis.summary_en: Influenza antivirals can directly benefit treated individuals by reducing the risk of some influenza-associated complications when initiated soon after symptom onset. The supplied evidence does not clearly state the study design, setting, or study population. Using a compartmental framework, we modeled population-level reductions in influenza-associated hospitalizations given potential direct and indirect effects of influenza antivirals in the United States. From reported patterns of care-seeking, antiviral prescribing, and treatment adherence, we estimated 1.1-9.7% of symptomatic individuals initiate and adhere to prompt antiviral treatment. For example, up to 3.8% of hospitalizations were prevented when antivirals reduced hospitalization risk and onward transmission by 20%. More substantial impacts (for example, preventing >20% of hospitalizations) were only achieved by increasing initiation and adherence to prompt treatment beyond typically observed levels. Assuming antivirals had direct and indirect effects generated slightly larger impacts.

title: Molecular Surveillance Finds No Influenza A Infection in Domestic Cats in Dhaka

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza A virus (IAV) is a zoonotic pathogen with a broad host range, including birds, humans, and various mammalian species. Domestic cats have been documented as incidental hosts, particularly in regions with ongoing avian influenza outbreaks.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Cats are important companion animals in Dhaka, Bangladesh; however, data on IAV infection in this population are limited. This study aimed to investigate the presence of IAV in domestic cats in Dhaka through molecular surveillance.
analysis.methods: A total of 50 nasal swab samples were collected from domestic cats with mild respiratory signs presented from different areas of Dhaka city. Samples were tested for IAV using real-time reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) targeting the matrix (M) gene.
analysis.main_results: All 50 samples tested negative for IAV.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: No evidence of IAV infection was found within the sampled population, suggesting low or no detectable zoonotic risk from domestic cats during the study period.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings provide baseline data on IAV surveillance in domestic cats in Dhaka.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: However, given the limited sample size and sampling period, larger longitudinal surveillance studies are warranted to better assess the potential for IAV spillover in high-risk settings.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted molecular surveillance of influenza A virus (IAV) in domestic cats in Dhaka, Bangladesh, to assess the potential for zoonotic transmission. A total of 50 nasal swab samples were collected from cats with mild respiratory signs and tested using qRT-PCR targeting the matrix (M) gene. All samples tested negative for IAV, indicating no detectable infection in the sampled population. The findings suggest a low zoonotic risk from domestic cats in Dhaka during the study period, but the limited sample size and short sampling period highlight the need for larger, longitudinal studies to better understand IAV spillover dynamics. These results contribute baseline data for IAV surveillance in domestic cats and may inform future public health strategies in the region.

title: Effectiveness of the 2025–2026 seasonal influenza vaccine among U.S. veterans: an observational study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of the 2025–2026 seasonal influenza vaccine among U.S. veterans, given the emergence of a newly antigenically distinct influenza A(H3N2) subclade K. The background highlights the variability in vaccine effectiveness due to antigenic mismatch between the vaccine and circulating strains.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Department of Veterans Affairs electronic health records to conduct a series of 24 sequential 7-day target trials among veterans with an in-person primary care visit between September 15, 2025, and February 28, 2026, comparing vaccinated and unvaccinated participants.
analysis.methods: The study defined exposure as receipt of the 2025–2026 seasonal influenza vaccine on the date of an eligible primary care visit. The primary outcome was a composite of seasonal influenza–associated emergency department visit or hospitalization. Vaccine effectiveness was estimated using discrete-time survival models with inverse-probability-of-treatment and inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting.
analysis.main_results: The 2025–2026 vaccine was associated with a lower risk of the composite outcome (VE, 21.95%; 95% CI, 16.08%–27.65%), influenza-associated emergency department visits (VE, 22.25%; 95% CI, 16.38%–27.94%), and influenza-associated hospitalizations (VE, 31.84%; 95% CI, 14.77%–46.27%). These results were consistent across subgroups and sensitivity analyses.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found that the 2025–2026 vaccine was associated with reductions in influenza-associated emergency department visits and hospitalizations, but its effectiveness was lower than in the immediately preceding season.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide contemporary, season-specific evidence supporting the continued use of seasonal influenza vaccination to prevent clinically important influenza outcomes.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study design limitations include the observational nature of the data and potential confounding factors. The evidence strength is moderate due to the observational design and the need for further research to confirm these findings.

analysis.summary_en: The study evaluated the effectiveness of the 2025–2026 seasonal influenza vaccine among U.S. veterans, finding it associated with reduced risk of emergency department visits and hospitalizations, but with lower effectiveness compared to the previous season.

title: AXL mediates influenza A virus entry and drives virus-induced inflammation.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Influenza A virus (IAV) infection remains a persistent global health challenge with limited antiviral drugs. Viral entry represents a potential multifaceted target for antiviral intervention; however, there is a limited number of approved inhibitors that effectively prevent IAV entry.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Here, we identify the receptor tyrosine kinase AXL as an IAV functional entry factor with dual roles in viral invasion and host immune modulation.
analysis.methods: Mechanistically, AXL mediates IAV invasion via the GAS6-AXL-AKT/ERK signalling axis and distinct endocytic pathways: clathrin-mediated endocytosis in epithelial cells and macropinocytosis-dominated endocytosis in alveolar macrophages.
analysis.main_results: Although AXL has been previously reported as a negative regulator of inflammation, we reveal that its inhibition simultaneously reduces viral entry and virus-induced inflammatory responses.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Consistently, AXL knockout mice or early administration of an AXL inhibitor during infection markedly reduced pulmonary viral loads, attenuated virus-induced cytokine production and lung pathology, and improved survival.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Beyond IAV, AXL also contributes to the entry of SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV, and human metapneumovirus (hMPV), suggesting its potential as a broad-spectrum host-directed antiviral target.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Collectively, our findings provide the first in vivo and in vitro evidence that AXL functions dually as a viral entry factor and immune modulator, highlighting its promise as a therapeutic target to block infection and control virus-induced inflammation.

analysis.summary_en: This study identifies AXL as a functional entry factor for influenza A virus (IAV) with dual roles in viral invasion and host immune modulation. The research highlights the potential of targeting AXL to block IAV infection and control virus-induced inflammation. The findings reveal that AXL inhibition reduces both viral entry and inflammatory responses, supported by in vivo and in vitro experiments. AXL knockout mice and early inhibitor administration showed reduced viral loads, attenuated cytokine production, and improved survival. These results suggest AXL as a promising therapeutic target for seasonal influenza, with implications for antiviral strategies. However, the study's evidence is limited to the specific context of IAV, and broader applications to other viruses require further investigation.

title: Leveraging perturbations to infer the population dynamics of human rhinovirus and interaction of influenza A virus.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand how the dynamics of human rhinovirus and influenza A virus interact within human populations, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. This is important because many respiratory pathogens co-circulate within human populations, and how their community structure shapes disease dynamics remains poorly understood.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used surveillance time series data from the US and Canada during the COVID-19 pandemic to investigate the population dynamics of human rhinovirus and the potential interference of influenza A virus. The analysis was conducted using a Bayesian framework.
analysis.methods: A Bayesian framework was employed to simulate and analyze the impact of exogenous perturbations on the dynamics of human rhinovirus and influenza A virus. The framework was then applied to real surveillance data to estimate key parameters of rhinovirus and assess the influence of influenza A virus.
analysis.main_results: The study found that exogenous perturbations can be a powerful tool to disentangle the contribution of pathogen interaction from other epidemiological factors. However, the analysis of surveillance data did not provide conclusive support for an influence of influenza A virus on the population dynamics of human rhinovirus.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted their findings as novel insights into the complex interplay between respiratory pathogens, leveraging a unique natural experiment provided by the COVID-19 pandemic. They highlighted the potential of using exogenous perturbations to better understand pathogen dynamics.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform surveillance and public health strategies by providing a method to better understand the dynamics of respiratory pathogens. This can help in the development of targeted interventions and policies to manage the spread of these viruses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the challenge of investigating polymicrobial dynamics due to confounding factors such as differing seasonality. The evidence strength is moderate, as the study relies on surveillance data and simulations, which may have some limitations in capturing all real-world complexities.

analysis.summary_en: This study used a Bayesian framework to investigate the population dynamics of human rhinovirus and the potential interference of influenza A virus during the COVID-19 pandemic. The findings suggest that exogenous perturbations can help disentangle pathogen interactions, but no conclusive support was found for influenza A virus influencing rhinovirus dynamics.

title: Induction of HAMP by Influenza A Virus in the LncRNA-155-Deficient Host Contributes to Suppression of Antiviral Innate Immunity

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate the molecular mechanism by which lncRNA-155 modulates antiviral innate immunity against influenza A virus (IAV). The background highlights the persistent pandemic potential of IAV and the critical role of long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) in antiviral immunity, with a focus on understanding how lncRNA-155 enhances immune responses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study utilized RNA-sequencing analysis in lncRNA-155-deficient mice to examine the transcriptional signature related to IAV-induced interferon-β (IFN-β) expression and interferon-stimulated genes. It also included functional analysis in animal tissues and cells to assess the impact of HAMP expression on IAV replication.
analysis.methods: RNA-sequencing analysis was conducted to identify the transcriptional signature of lncRNA-155-deficient mice in response to IAV infection. Functional analysis involved knockdown and overexpression of HAMP in animal tissues and cells to evaluate its effect on IAV replication and antiviral responses.
analysis.main_results: The results showed that lncRNA-155 functions as a negative regulator of HAMP expression, with a robust upregulation of HAMP observed in lncRNA-155-deficient tissues and cells upon IAV infection. HAMP overexpression significantly inhibited IAV-induced IFN-β production and interferon-stimulated genes expression, while knockdown of HAMP reduced viral replication by enhancing antiviral responses.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that lncRNA-155 suppresses HAMP to augment antiviral immunity, identifying a novel lncRNA-155/HAMP axis that plays a critical role in modulating the innate immune response to IAV. This finding provides new insights into the regulatory mechanisms of antiviral immunity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings may inform the development of therapeutic strategies targeting the lncRNA-155/HAMP axis to enhance antiviral innate immunity against seasonal influenza viruses. They also highlight the importance of understanding viral modulation of host immune responses for improved vaccine and treatment design.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on animal models and the lack of direct clinical evidence. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on RNA-sequencing and functional analysis in mice, which may not fully translate to human contexts.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the molecular mechanism by which lncRNA-155 modulates antiviral innate immunity against influenza A virus (IAV). It identifies lncRNA-155 as a negative regulator of HAMP expression, with HAMP overexpression suppressing antiviral responses and promoting IAV replication. The findings reveal a novel lncRNA-155/HAMP axis that enhances antiviral immunity by inhibiting HAMP. These results may inform future therapeutic strategies targeting this axis to improve immune responses against seasonal influenza viruses. However, the study is limited to animal models, and the evidence is moderate due to the absence of direct clinical data.

title: mRNA-based seasonal influenza vaccines: an overview of immunogenicity, efficacy, and safety

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study addresses the limitations of current seasonal influenza vaccines, which are primarily produced in eggs, and explores the potential of mRNA technology to overcome these challenges. The rationale is based on the need for more effective and adaptable vaccine platforms.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is an overview of clinical trials evaluating the immunogenicity, efficacy, and safety of standalone and combination mRNA influenza vaccines. It includes vaccines such as Moderna’s mRNA-1010 and Pfizer’s modified-nucleoside RNA candidate, as well as Moderna’s combination influenza and COVID-19 vaccine, mRNA-1083.
analysis.methods: The study synthesizes data from clinical trials, focusing on the immunogenicity, efficacy, and safety of mRNA vaccines. It includes analysis of humoral and cell-mediated immune responses, relative efficacy comparisons, and safety profiles against standard-dose vaccines.
analysis.main_results: An optimized mRNA-1010 formulation demonstrated a relative efficacy of 26.6% (95% CI: 16.7%, 35.4%) in adults aged ≥50 years. Pfizer’s first-generation quadrivalent modRNA candidate showed 34.5% (95% CI: 7.4%, 53.9%) relative efficacy in younger adults (18–64 years) but failed to show non-inferiority in older adults (≥65 years), with a relative efficacy of −5.8% (95% CI: −47.2%, 23.8%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that mRNA-based vaccines can induce robust immune responses, particularly against influenza A strains, and represent a significant technological advancement. However, their efficacy relative to enhanced formulations for older adults remains uncertain.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results inform the development and implementation of mRNA vaccines for seasonal influenza, highlighting their potential for improved immunogenicity and safety, while also emphasizing the need for further studies to compare them with existing enhanced formulations.

title: A case report series of influenza A virus-induced pulmonary disease with diverse clinical manifestations

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to report on the clinical manifestations and outcomes of IAV-induced pulmonary disease in patients with and without underlying chronic respiratory diseases, addressing the need for understanding the diverse clinical presentations of IAV infection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved three cases of IAV-associated pulmonary disease, including two elderly men with COPD and one middle-aged man without underlying disease, observed over unspecified dates at unspecified centres.
analysis.methods: The study described the clinical presentation, imaging findings, and treatment responses of three patients with IAV-induced pulmonary disease, focusing on respiratory support and antimicrobial therapy.
analysis.main_results: The study observed that two patients with COPD experienced persistent AHR and ventilatory failure despite aggressive treatment, while the patient without underlying disease recovered with high-flow nasal oxygen therapy alone.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that underlying respiratory status significantly influenced the clinical course of IAV-associated AHR, with patients with COPD showing more persistent symptoms compared to the patient without chronic respiratory disease.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that respiratory status may play a critical role in the clinical outcomes of IAV-associated AHR, highlighting the need for tailored treatment approaches in patients with underlying respiratory conditions.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the small sample size and lack of randomization, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. The evidence strength is moderate due to the observational nature of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This case series reported on three patients with IAV-induced pulmonary disease, showing that patients with COPD experienced more persistent AHR and ventilatory failure compared to the patient without underlying disease, who recovered with high-flow nasal oxygen therapy.

title: Emergence and spread of NA-I223V and NA-S247N double-mutant A(H1N1)pdm09 influenza viruses with reduced oseltamivir susceptibility in the Netherlands and beyond, 2023 to 2026

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the emergence, spread and antiviral susceptibility of A(H1N1)pdm09 influenza viruses with specific double mutations in the Netherlands and other regions from 2023 to 2026.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study tracked the emergence and spread of A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses with double mutations NA-I223V and NA-S247N in the Netherlands and other countries between 2023 and 2026, noting their re-emergence and expansion in different NA-clades.
analysis.methods: The study involved genomic surveillance and phenotypic analysis of influenza viruses, including testing for oseltamivir susceptibility using median inhibition values.
analysis.main_results: Dutch double mutants from both 2023/24 and 2025/26 seasons showed median 12- and 13-fold reduced inhibition by oseltamivir, respectively.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight the dynamic evolution of antiviral resistance in seasonal influenza viruses, particularly in A(H1N1)pdm09 strains with specific double mutations.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results emphasize the importance of continuous genomic and phenotypic monitoring to detect and respond to emerging antiviral resistance patterns in seasonal influenza viruses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on observational data from genomic surveillance and phenotypic testing, which may be subject to limitations in capturing full epidemiological context and causal relationships.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the emergence and spread of A(H1N1)pdm09 influenza viruses with double mutations NA-I223V and NA-S247N in the Netherlands and other regions from 2023 to 2026. It reports that these double mutants showed reduced susceptibility to oseltamivir, with median inhibition values of 12- and 13-fold lower in the two seasons. The findings underscore the need for ongoing genomic and phenotypic monitoring of antiviral resistance in seasonal influenza viruses. The study's reliance on observational data and phenotypic testing may limit the depth of causal interpretation, but the evidence is strong due to the direct reporting of resistance measurements. The results have implications for public health strategies, particularly in tracking and managing antiviral resistance in seasonal influenza strains.

title: ATTITUDES AND PRACTICES TOWARDS COVID-19 AND SEASONAL FLU VACCINES AND VACCINATION IN THE GENERAL POPULATION AND AMONG MEDICAL PROFESSIONALS

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate attitudes towards COVID-19 and seasonal influenza vaccination among the general population and individuals with a medical background.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Participants generally expressed favourable attitudes towards regular COVID-19 vaccination. The profile of the typical participant was an employed woman with tertiary education, living with another person in an urban area and reporting generally good health.
analysis.methods: A questionnaire was developed to collect sociodemographic data, personal health information, vaccination status, and information on participants’ attitudes towards and knowledge of vaccines.
analysis.main_results: The results showed no apparent differences between participants with and without a medical background regarding vaccine choice, the decision to receive a third dose, or seasonal influenza vaccination.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as indicating that attitudes towards vaccination are similar across medical professionals and the general population, highlighting a novel observation about public perception of vaccines.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform public health strategies by suggesting that targeted communication efforts may not need to differentiate between medical professionals and the general population in promoting vaccination.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on self-reported data and its abstract-only nature, which may affect the strength of the evidence.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated attitudes towards COVID-19 and seasonal influenza vaccination among the general population and medical professionals. It found that there were no apparent differences in vaccine choice, third-dose decisions, or seasonal influenza vaccination between the two groups. The research highlights the importance of understanding public perception of vaccines, which can inform public health strategies. However, the study is limited by its reliance on self-reported data and its abstract-only nature, which may affect the reliability of the findings. The results suggest that attitudes towards vaccination are consistent across different professional backgrounds, indicating a potential for uniform messaging in health promotion.

title: A nanoemulsion-adjuvanted trivalent neuraminidase vaccine confers cross-protection against divergent influenza viruses

analysis.research_question_and_background: Neuraminidase (NA), a relatively conserved surface antigen of influenza viruses, is a promising target for UIV design.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The supplied evidence does not clearly state the study design, setting, or study population.
analysis.methods: The supplied evidence does not clearly state the core experimental, analytical, or statistical methods.
analysis.main_results: Immunogenicity evaluation of N2NA (derived from H3N2) in mice demonstrated that nanoemulsion (NE) adjuvant significantly enhanced NA-inhibiting (NI) antibody titers, CD4 T cell responses, and the numbers of IL-2-, IL-4- and IFN-γ-secreting lymphocytes compared to the unadjuvanted vaccine.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Collectively, these findings support the efficacy of a multivalent NA-based vaccine strategy and highlight its strong potential as a candidate UIV.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Developing universal influenza vaccines (UIVs) capable of eliciting broad protection remains a critical public health priority.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Furthermore, the NE-adjuvanted trivalent NA vaccine (N1+N2+BV) elicited robust humoral and cellular immunity and provided effective protection in mice against two H1N1, two B/Victoria, and one H5N1 strain.

analysis.summary_en: Neuraminidase (NA), a relatively conserved surface antigen of influenza viruses, is a promising target for UIV design. The supplied evidence does not clearly state the study design, setting, or study population. The supplied evidence does not clearly state the core experimental, analytical, or statistical methods. Immunogenicity evaluation of N2NA (derived from H3N2) in mice demonstrated that nanoemulsion (NE) adjuvant significantly enhanced NA-inhibiting (NI) antibody titers, CD4 T cell responses, and the numbers of IL-2-, IL-4- and IFN-γ-secreting lymphocytes compared to the unadjuvanted vaccine. Collectively, these findings support the efficacy of a multivalent NA-based vaccine strategy and highlight its strong potential as a candidate UIV. Developing universal influenza vaccines (UIVs) capable of eliciting broad protection remains a critical public health priority. Furthermore, the NE-adjuvanted trivalent NA vaccine (N1+N2+BV) elicited robust humoral and cellular immunity and provided effective protection in mice against two H1N1, two B/Victoria, and one H5N1 strain.

title: Enhanced induction of inflammatory cytokines in human lung cells infected with highly pathogenic recent H5N1/2024 avian influenza virus

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate the infectivity and cytokine induction in human lung cells infected with highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza viruses compared to seasonal H3N2 influenza viruses, as HP H5N1 viruses are zoonotic pathogens and pro-inflammatory cytokines are thought to contribute to severe clinical symptoms in infected individuals.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study compared the infectivity and cytokine induction in primary human lung cells infected with highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza viruses and seasonal H3N2 influenza viruses. The research was conducted using human lung cells and MDCK cells to measure viral titers.
analysis.methods: Quantitative real-time PCR was used to detect cytokine gene induction in infected primary human lung cells, and MDCK cells were employed to measure viral titers in the supernatants of infected cells by log10TCID50/ml.
analysis.main_results: Highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza viruses induced higher viral titers than seasonal H3N2 influenza viruses in supernatants of primary human lung cells. Additionally, they induced pro-inflammatory cytokine genes such as IL-23, IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8 at significantly higher levels than seasonal H3N2 influenza viruses.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors suggest that the high viral replication and cytokine induction in human lung cells infected with HP H5N1 avian influenza viruses may enhance pathogenicity in infected humans compared to seasonal H3N2 influenza viruses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the potential for HP H5N1 avian influenza viruses to cause more severe disease in humans than seasonal H3N2 influenza viruses, which may inform surveillance, diagnosis, and the development of targeted antiviral strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study does not provide detailed statistical analyses or controls for confounding variables, and the evidence is based on a single comparison between HP H5N1 and seasonal H3N2 influenza viruses, which limits the generalizability of the findings. The evidence is moderate in strength.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the infectivity and cytokine induction in human lung cells infected with highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza viruses compared to seasonal H3N2 influenza viruses. The research found that HP H5N1 viruses induced higher viral titers and significantly increased the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokine genes such as IL-23, IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8 in human lung cells. These results suggest that HP H5N1 may lead to more severe disease in humans than seasonal H3N2 viruses. The study used quantitative real-time PCR and MDCK cells to measure viral titers and cytokine induction. While the findings provide insights into the pathogenic potential of HP H5N1, the lack of detailed statistical analyses and controls limits the confidence in the conclusions. The evidence is moderate in strength.

title: Clinical impact of baloxavir-induced PA I38T/M substitutions in diverse influenza populations: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines seasonal influenza and the clinical impact of baloxavir‐induced PA I38T/M substitutions, aiming to quantify mutation incidence and associated disease outcomes in pediatric and adult patients.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A systematic review and meta‐analysis of prospective clinical trials was performed, selecting studies that reported the pooled incidence of PA I38T/M substitutions and time to illness alleviation as primary outcomes.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The pooled incidence of PA I38T/M substitutions was 10.5% (95% CI 0.0%–21.1%) with substantial heterogeneity, and the overall delay in time to illness alleviation was non‐significant (15.47 h, 95% CI ‐40.96 to 71.91, P = 0.359); however, pediatric cohorts showed higher mutation rates and longer clinical delays, and the authors conclude that these substitutions are linked to notable virological rebound and delayed recovery, especially in children.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: High heterogeneity (I2 = 94.6% for incidence, I2 = 81.8% for TTIA) and divergent subgroup effects indicate limited consistency across studies, with adult data showing modest impact while pediatric data reveal pronounced delays, highlighting a need for more robust, age‐stratified investigations.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The findings underscore the need for age‐specific resistance monitoring and suggest evaluating combination antiviral regimens to curb resistance emergence, reflecting broader public‐health concerns about baloxavir‐driven PA mutations.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta‐analysis evaluated the incidence and clinical consequences of baloxavir‐induced PA I38T/M substitutions in seasonal influenza across pediatric and adult populations. The pooled incidence was 10.5% (95% CI 0.0%–21.1%) with considerable heterogeneity, and overall time to illness alleviation showed a non‐significant delay, though children experienced markedly longer delays and higher mutation rates. The authors conclude that these substitutions contribute to virological rebound and delayed recovery, especially in children. High heterogeneity and divergent subgroup results reveal gaps in consistent evidence, calling for more age‐focused studies. Implications include the necessity for age‐specific resistance surveillance and exploration of combination antiviral therapies to mitigate resistance development.

title: Preclinical toxicity and immunogenicity of a quadrivalent recombinant influenza hemagglutinin vaccine (SCVC101) in rhesus monkeys.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate the toxicity and immunogenicity of SCVC101 in rhesus monkeys. The background is the need for a novel recombinant hemagglutinin (rHA) protein-based quadrivalent seasonal influenza vaccine containing HA gene sequences of A/Wisconsin/588/2019 (H1N1) pdm09-like virus, A/Cambodia/e0826360/2020 (H3N2)-like virus, B/Washington/02/2019 (B/Victoria lineage)-like virus, and B/Phuket/3073/2013 (B/Yamagata).
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted under Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) conditions in rhesus monkeys, with intramuscular administrations of two distinct dose levels (15 μg and 45 μg of rHA per virus strain) during weeks 0, 3, and 6 of the experimental protocol.
analysis.methods: Under GLP conditions, rhesus monkeys received intramuscular administrations of two distinct dose levels (15 μg and 45 μg of rHA per virus strain) during weeks 0, 3, and 6 of the experimental protocol.
analysis.main_results: The results showed that SCVC101 vaccination elicited a strong specific binding antibody and neutralizing antibodies in the low- and high-dose vaccine groups. Significant immune responses to influenza viruses were demonstrated in rhesus monkeys.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: No significant systemic toxicities or abnormal cardiovascular and respiratory events were observed after three doses of SCVC101 in rhesus monkeys. Therefore, our regulatory toxicology research demonstrates strong immunogenicity and a favorable safety profile of the SCVC101 vaccine.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that SCVC101 is a promising candidate for further development as a quadrivalent influenza vaccine, with strong immunogenicity and a favorable safety profile in rhesus monkeys.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the use of rhesus monkeys as a model, which may not fully represent human responses. The sample size is small, and the study was conducted under GLP conditions, which may not reflect real-world scenarios. The evidence strength is moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the toxicity and immunogenicity of SCVC101, a quadrivalent recombinant hemagglutinin vaccine, in rhesus monkeys. The vaccine elicited strong immune responses without significant toxicities, suggesting it is a promising candidate for further development.
